en: The Classical proper: the bishop pins f6 before pushing e5.
One White player in five develops the queen's knight first, and the course only saw Nf3. The difference matters: the c3 knight blocks the c2 pawn, and so the c4 break.
The bishop before the knights — one White player in seven, and the course had not planned for it. It eyes h7, but nothing is there yet.
We play our move anyway: with no pawn on d4, the e5 push leaves us comfortable.
Two White players in three exchange here, and the course only planned for e5. It was the repertoire's biggest gap: the Exchange Variation via this move order simply did not exist.
Four White players in ten support the centre with d4 rather than c3, and the course only planned for c3.
We recapture with the e-pawn, which solves the French's eternal problem at a stroke: the c8 bishop is no longer shut in. The position is symmetrical and perfectly playable.
White has no active plan left. The Exchange has a drawish reputation: it is deserved as soon as White gives up on c4.
We hit the centre while it is unsupported. In the Exchange, whoever breaks first and profitably takes the initiative.
We push rather than trade: the d3 bishop must retreat, and our queenside majority gets a head start.
We take at once: without c3, White must recapture with a piece, and their advanced centre loses its anchor.
The French's signature break: we attack the head of White's pawn chain. This is where the game is decided, and the moment must not be missed.
Hypermodern and sharp: Black lets White build a big centre… then attacks it from behind with …Bg7, …c5 and pressure on d4.

One game in six, and the course started from 2.c4. The Grünfeld assumes a White centre to demolish: without c4 there is none.
The Grünfeld move: strike the centre instead of just fianchettoing as in the King's Indian.
A quiet development: the bishop comes out before e3. Black still hits with …c5.
The fianchetto: White forgoes the big centre for positional play around d5.
White's centre is huge but will become a target: …c5 is coming.
The Russian System: the queen hits d5 and b7. Black takes on c4 with counterplay.
We occupy rather than counterattack. A deliberate change of plan: against a system, take the space.
…d5 before …g6: if c4 arrives we transpose into an Exchange Grünfeld via …g6; otherwise we have a sound structure.
The bishop goes to c4 and eyes f7. Two worlds in one: the slow, positional Giuoco Pianissimo, and the tactical universe of the Two Knights (Fried Liver, Traxler) and the Evans Gambit.

Black defends e5 with a pawn and declines the whole debate. A 1.e4 e5 course must answer it: this is an entry point, not a sideline.
The Petrov: instead of defending e5, Black attacks e4. Reputedly dry, it's common — and the course said nothing about it.
The Italian bishop: it presses f7, Black's soft spot.
The Giuoco Piano: the bishops face off; a manoeuvring game lies ahead.
The Two Knights: instead of …Bc5, Black hits e4. Things get sharp.
The Hungarian: a modest, solid choice to sidestep all the tactical venom.
A waiting move — one Black player in seven — stopping Ng5 but developing nothing. The course only planned for …Bc5, …Nf6 and …Be7.
Preparing d4 and a c2 retreat for the bishop.
The Evans Gambit: a pawn to deflect the c5 bishop and unleash development.
Opening the centre at once: open play, often transposing to the Scotch Gambit.
More than one Black player in four props up e5 with the pawn, and the course only saw …Nf6. It is solid, but it leaves the centre to White for one move longer.
The modern plan: d3, then the famous Nbd2-f1-g3 tour and a kingside attack.
The classical break: opening the centre instead of the slow d3 plan.
Each side prepares queenside expansion (…b5 / a4).
The Møller Attack: offering a pawn for rapid development and initiative.
The aggressive move: hitting f7 at once.
The only good defence: counterattack rather than defend f7.
The Traxler: Black ignores the f7 threat and hits f2 in return! Guaranteed chaos.
The main line: the knight hits the c4 bishop; Black gives a pawn for the initiative.
The Fritz: sharper than …Na5, aiming for a direct attack.
The Ulvestad: …b5 kicks the bishop before regaining d5. Very sharp.
Recapturing on d5 is risky: it allows the Fried Liver sacrifice.
The Fried Liver sacrifice! Black's king is dragged out; the attack is very dangerous in practice.
Taking f7 leads to the wildest complications; Bxf7+ is the safer route.
The most played retreat — two Black players in five — and the course only knew …Ba5. The bishop returns to the most active diagonal, but it will be harried there.
Strike at once. The Philidor is solid but cramped: giving it time to breathe would be doing it a favour.
Nearly six Black players in ten release the tension, and the course only saw …Nd7. They hand us the centre to avoid being squeezed.
Black is sound but has neither space nor counterplay. Our plan is simple: Re1, a4, and squeeze.
We take. The immediate …Nxe4 is the classic blunder: Qe2 then wins the queen or a piece via the discovered check.
The classic Petrov MISTAKE, and two Black players in five make it: they defend the e5 knight instead of kicking it with …d6. The course only planned for …d6.
The knight retreats — never Nxf7, which gives only two pawns for a piece.
We punish the slow move with the centre: every move spent not developing is a move we spend opening the position.
The queen trade is no peaceful simplification: Black recaptures with the KING and loses castling. …h6 ends up costing them their king's safety.
Here is why the b-pawn was given: White builds a centre Black cannot contest, and gains a tempo on the bishop at the same time.
The sequence to know, because it is forced and wins a pawn outright: Black regains it with checks, but their queen wanders while we castle.
We trade before they can fix it: their c-pawns are doubled, and the e4 pawn will advance with no knight to stop it.
The pawn drives off the f6 knight, the only defender of the coming castled position. White is close to winning material in practice — the price of …Nc6.
The knight retreats rather than trade: …c5 has weakened d5 and b5, two squares our pieces will occupy in peace.
The romantic gambit par excellence: a pawn for a strong centre, an open f-file and an immediate attack. From the Kieseritzky to the Muzio sacrifice, pure fire.

The modern, soundest defence: Black gives the pawn back for clear play.
Black clings to the f4 pawn — the sharpest line.
The modern defence in the accepted gambit: instead of clinging with …g5, Black gives back and develops.

The soundest move: Black consolidates before going for …g5. One player in seven, and the course only planned for the check …Qh4+.
Black attacks e4 instead of clinging to the f4 pawn. The modern way to meet the Bishop's Gambit, and the course said nothing about it.
Simple development. One player in eight, missing from the course.
Undermine the advanced e4 pawn rather than let it cramp development.
They accept after all, one move later — and transpose into the previous line, where d4 and then d5 are waiting.
Pin the defender of e5 before resolving the tension: that move order is what gives the edge.
No forcing. It becomes a king's pawn game where our f4 gains space without conceding anything.
The reflex check. After g3, the queen has lost two tempi and our development is ahead.
The knight is back on g1 — humiliating but correct: it will re-emerge via e2, and White's centre is worth the lost time.
We develop while covering h4: no more check to fear, and the knight watches g5, where Black wants to push.
We defend e4 with a piece, without touching a pawn: the centre stays whole and development continues.
Black doubles our pawns to hold e4. In exchange we get the b-file and two bishops against a king that has lost its f-pawn.
The check that defines the Bishop's Gambit: there is no knight on f3 to block it, and White's king must move. That is the accepted price of 3.Bc4.
The king steps aside, and it is no disaster: the h1 rook will come out via g1 once the g-pawn moves, and Black will have spent their queen on early sorties.
The push that turns everything around: the pawn hits the c6 knight at the exact moment Black has committed on the kingside. What follows is forced and must be known.
A setup to play against anything starting …e6 or …d5: Nf3, g3, Bg2, 0-0, d3, e4. Attack on the kingside with e5, Nf1-h2-g4 and f4.

One Black player in four plays this here, and the chapter started from …Nf6. Black takes queenside space — precisely the wing we are going to concede.
Black releases the tension at once. This is the second most played move here, and the course said nothing about it.
The rook supports the e5 push, which closes the centre and starts the attack. It is the pivot move of the whole system.
Each side attacks on its wing: Black on the left, White with e5 then Nf1-h2-g4.
Black prepares …e5 to seize the centre first. The chapter only saw …Nf6.
The next most common order after …Nc6, and it wasn't covered either.
e5 must be over-defended first: 10.Nf1 at once drops the pawn to …Ndxe5!, backed up by the c7 queen.
Nearly one Sicilian player in three plays …d6 before developing the knight, and the chapter started from …Nc6.
The Paulsen Sicilian. The chapter only planned for …Nc6 and …d6 — yet this is one player in six's choice.
Black prepares …d5 to contest the centre. The chapter only knew …g6.
The system move: we give up d4 and all Sicilian theory. The game will be played on our terms.
A symmetrical structure — but we're the ones who know the plan: Nbd2, Re1, e5, then Nf1-h2-g4.
No cause for alarm: the bishop heads to g2 and will target the d5 pawn as soon as it advances.
The system's moment: we hit d5 in the centre. After the trade, the g2 bishop breathes at last.
Seven Black players in ten develop this knight here, and the chapter started from …Nf6. They build the big centre; we are going to let it freeze.
Here, exceptionally, d4 is right: Black has already committed to …c5 and …e6, and the structure is a Catalan one, not a system where we bide our time.
We contest nothing on the queenside: the King's Indian Attack plan is always the same — castle, play e5, then attack on the king. Letting the opponent expand over there is part of the bargain.
Recapture with the PAWN, not the knight: the d-file opens for us, and the d2 knight stays free to go to c4 or f3 depending on what Black does.
The position looks symmetrical, but every one of our pieces eyes Black's castled king — and we are a tempo ahead.
We stay in the system. The engine prefers 3.d4 and the Open Sicilian, but that is a different repertoire: here we want the same plan every game, not twenty variations to revise.
The king first, as always in this system. Black's centre is going nowhere, and every move they spend on it is a move they do not spend on their king.
The signature break: we hit the centre from the flank, at a distance, having never faced it head-on.
The quiet move that holds everything: the queen supports e4 without blocking anyone, and prepares e5 — the push that closes the centre and unleashes the attack.
And there is the whole system: closed centre, Black's knight pushed back, and every piece of ours aimed at their king.
Give White the centre, then blow it up with …e5 and a kingside pawn storm (…f5-f4-g4). The attacker's opening.

Stronger than Nge2: White pushes BEFORE developing, and …Bxg4 no longer works.
The demolition sacrifice: the g4 pawn props up White's whole centre. After fxg4, …Ncxe4 wins everything back and the white king is left bare.
Black must block: letting h4-h5 open the h-file would be fatal to the king.
White fianchettoes too: the most positional line, fewer fireworks.
The Averbakh: the g5 bishop discourages …e5 (the pin). Black plays …c5.
We keep our setup. Against the London it even has a plus: the f4 bishop has no target and must retreat once …Nh5 comes.
THE move to know: we hunt White's good bishop. If it goes to g3, …Nxg3 doubles the pawns; if it holds e5, …f6 evicts it.
And c4 arrives after all: we're back in the King's Indian by another route. You just had to keep your nerve.
The mirror of the King's Gambit, but for Black: …f5 on move two, all-or-nothing play. Objectively risky, but a nightmare for the unprepared.
